paper_title: DR Pixel: Page-Native Deep Research with Vision-Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Complex documents such as scientific papers contain rich information in tables, figures, and equations; however, existing deep research (DR) agents typically reduce papers to OCR-extracted text. We instead ask whether vision-language models (VLMs) can enable page-native deep research: directly retrieving and reasoning over rendered document page images. We introduce DR Pixel, the first open-source end-to-end multimodal DR agent that uses rendered page images as its sole retrieval and reasoning unit, operating over a corpus of 1.06M pages. To evaluate this setting, we construct DRPixelBench, a benchmark on scientific papers requiring reasoning over text, figures, tables, and equations. Surprisingly, page-native DR already works well without training, outperforming OCR-based baselines across state-of-the-art models like GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Qwen3.6-27B, while requiring fewer tool calls. We next turn to DR training. A key challenge is that teacher trajectories for agentic supervised finetuning are noisy, mixing critical reasoning and action steps with redundant or failed attempts. To address this, we introduce counterfactual credit reweighting, a fine-grained credit assignment method that weights individual reasoning and action steps by their counterfactual contribution to the final answer. Our training improves retrieval recall by about 15 points and final accuracy by over 10 points on DRPixelBench, and likewise outperforms the untrained baseline on four existing benchmarks. On out-of-distribution ViDoRe-V3, DR Pixel comes within 1.8 points of an oracle that is given the gold pages directly. Our results suggest that the conventional OCR-then-retrieve pipeline is not only unnecessary but suboptimal: directly retrieving and reasoning over visual document pages makes complex DR both more effective and more efficient.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Deep research (DR) agents answer complex information-seeking questions by iteratively searching, reading, and reasoning over large collections of evidence (OpenAI, 2025; Gemini, 2025; Li et al., 2025d;a). As DR expands beyond the open web into domains such as law, finance, and science, it increasingly operates over specialized document collections (Li et al., 2025b; Choi et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025a;b). These documents are inherently multimodal: critical evidence often lies not only in text, but also in tables, figures, charts, and equations. Yet, such documents are typically reduced to plain text: PDFs are linearized into text, and retrieval and reasoning operate entirely in text space. This introduces two key limitations. First, linearization discards or distorts visual structure, making information in figures, tables, or charts difficult or impossible to recover (Poznanski et al., 2025; Lo et al., 2023). Second, extraction and OCR errors propagate into downstream retrieval and reasoning (Zhang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026). This raises natural question: Can deep research instead be page-native, retrieving and reasoning directly over rendered document pages? In such an approach, each page remains an image: visual

We study this approach in the deep research regime, where answering query requires many rounds of retrieval and reasoning. To this end, we introduce DR PIXEL, the first open-source page-native multimodal DR agent that iteratively searches and reasons directly over 1.06M rendered pages from scientific papers. The first challenge is evaluation: existing DR benchmarks are either predominantly text-based (Chen et al., 2026; Xiong et al., 2026; Asai et al., 2024) or require relatively simple retrieval where single search already achieves high recall (Wang et al., 2025a; Tanaka et al., 2023). To bridge this gap, we introduce DRPIXELBENCH, comprising 500 questions over 1M pages of scientific papers. It combines complex deep research queries that require long chains of retrieval and reasoning with the visual reasoning demands of scientific papers, such as interpreting experimental results in figures and tables. Each question is grounded in gold page and paired with directly verifiable answer. We then instantiate page-native deep research as an end-to-end VLM agent. DR PIXEL indexes rendered pages directly with VLM embedding model (Li et al., 2026a), feeds retrieved images to the VLM agent, and maintains them as visual evidence throughout the trajectory, without ever being converted into plain text. The agent iteratively formulates queries, retrieves images, and reasons over evidence accumulated across turns to generate the final answer. Our evaluation on DRPIXELBENCH reveals consistent advantage of page-native DR over OCR-based pipelines, even without targeted training: page-native DR improves accuracy by 5.18.4 points across GPT-5.4 (OpenAI, 2026), Gemini-3.5-Flash (Google, 2026), and Qwen3.6-27B (Qwen, 2026), while using 20%30% fewer retrieval calls than OCR-based pipelines. Still, the open-weight Qwen3.6-27B lags behind closed models (40.1 vs. 51.9), motivating us to train DR PIXEL. key challenge is that demonstration traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) are often noisy, and are mix of useful and unhelpful steps: some are critical to reaching the correct answers, while others are redundant or failed attempts. To account for this, we introduce counterfactual credit reweighting: general recipe for DR training that weights each reasoning and action step by its contribution to the final answer. For each step, we estimate its contribution by removing it from the trajectory and assigning higher training weight when its removal degrades answer quality. Our training method significantly improves the performance: with Qwen3.6-27B, it improves accuracy by 12.0 points (30% relative) over the untrained model, and closes the gap to GPT-5.4. sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Deep research (DR) agents. DR agents tackle complex, multi-step information-seeking tasks through iterative search and synthesis (Yao et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025d;c; Shao et al., 2026). Recent work extends the pipeline to multimodal deep research by adding tools such as image search, reverse image search or cross-modality retrieval (Geng et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026). Most of them focus on open web, where text and images are retrieved separately through two different search tools (Tao et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Jiang et al., 2024). We instead target collection of documents (e.g., scientific papers), where answering complex questions often requires jointly interpreting text, tables, and figures on the same page, making separate text and image retrieval interfaces suboptimal. Page-native document retrieval. With rapid progress with vision-language models (VLMs), bypassing OCR pipelines and directly processing rendered document images has emerged as promising direction (Kim et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023; Blecher et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2026). Building on this, visual document retrieval retrieves rendered pages directly, established by ColPali and followed by increasingly capable visual retrievers (Faysse et al., 2025; Günther et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). More recent work extends this approach to further generate answers (Yu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; 2026) and add iterative retrieval (Wang et al., 2025b; Shen et al., 2026). However, these settings require relatively shallow search, e.g., on ViDoSeek (Wang et al., 2025a) and SlideVQA (Tanaka et al., 2023), single retrieval step already recalls the gold page in the top five for > 90% of questions (Wang et al., 2025a; Giouroukis et al., 2025). We instead study page-native deep research where complex queries require sustained search and reasoning over 1020 steps. Agent training. Broadly, agents that generate long action trajectories are commonly trained with outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) (Jin et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Shen et al., 2026), sometimes with rubrics (Shao et al., 2026), or through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on teacher-generated trajectories (Chen et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025a). Both provide limited credit assignment across trajectory: outcome-based RL assigns single reward to the rollout, and SFT imitates every teacher step regardless of its utility. Prior work has explored finer-grained supervision through process reward models that score each intermediate step (Lightman et al., 2023) or by leveraging tokenor step-level supervision coming from teacher model conditioned on privileged context (Meng & Chen, 2026; Wu et al., 2026), both during RL. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach that retains the simplicity of SFT: we reweight each agentic step by its counterfactual contribution to the final answer, estimated by removing the step and measuring the resulting change in answer quality.

sections.title: DRPixelBench
sections.content: We collect papers from arXiv and the openaccess proceedings of major conferences, and merge in the papers of AirQA (Huang et al., 2026), M3SciQA (Li et al., 2024) and IRPAPERS (Shorten et al., 2026) so that DRPIXELBENCH and these three benchmarks share one corpus of 99,055 papers. Table 1: DRPIXELBENCH is the only benchmark combining iterative search over large corpus (Agentic), multimodal evidence (MM), nontemplated questions (Non-templ.), and verifiable short answers (Verif.). Inspired by Dasigi et al. (2021), we generate each question from papers abstract rather than from its full text to keep it tied to the papers main contribution. As an abstract reports its findings with few supporting details, we first enrich it. Using Gemini-3.5-Flash (Google, 2026), we extract atomic facts from the full paper, such as comparison in table or trend in figure, and add them to the abstract. We then prompt the model to write question from the enriched abstract alone, so that the question is driven by curiosity rather than by evidence already in view. We further ask the model to locate the supporting evidence in the full paper and produce short-form answer. Depending on the form of this evidence, each question is labeled Text or Visual: Text question is answered from the running text, while Visual question requires table, figure, or equation. Each QA pair then undergoes four automatic checks to ensure that the question is plausible, the gold evidence is sufficient, non-textual evidence is necessary, and the answer cannot be recovered from parametric knowledge alone. Finally, human experts review the question and rewrite it for naturalness. The resulting DRPIXELBENCH contains 500 QA pairs. More details, including the data sources, parsing details, filter criteria, annotation details, and data statistics, are reported in A.

sections.title: 5 DR PIXEL TRAINING
sections.content: Having shown that page-native DR improves performance even without training, we next train DR PIXEL to further improve its capabilities. We denote the untrained model as DR PIXELBase and the trained model as DR PIXELTrained. We first describe the training method (5.1), then present the main results (5.2) and ablations (5.3).

We sample trajectories from GPT-5.4 on training questions generated using the same pipeline as 3, but without human rewriting or verification; and use them as training data. Naively imitating these unhelpful steps encourages excessive searching and inefficient use of the retrieval budget. sections.title: 5.3 ABLATION
sections.content: We next ablate on couple of key factors: corpus size, training data modalities and page resolutions. DR PIXELTrained is robust to corpus size. We scale the corpus from 20,000 to 99,000 papers while keeping the questions and gold documents fixed. As shown in Figure 4, page-hit rate declines for all models as the corpus grows, but DR PIXELTrained degrades more slowly, dropping by only 8.0 points compared with 12.5 for GPT-5.4. As result, its retrieval advantage over GPT-5.4 widens from 1.8 points at 20,000 papers to 6.3 points at 99,000, leading to final answer accuracy improvement. Downgrading page resolution buys efficiency at modest cost. In page-native deep research, page resolution determines the trade-off between visual fidelity and inference cost. Since processing high-resolution page images is expensive, we cap each rendered page at 1.05 megapixels, roughly 50% of its native resolution. As shown in Figure 5, this reduces input tokens by 30% to 48% across models, while accuracy drops by only 1.0 to 3.8 points. Output tokens rise slightly at lower resolution, but as they account for less than 25% of all tokens, the overall savings largely remain. 1 Even at this lower resolution, page retrieval outperforms OCR-based text retrieval by 2.7 to 7.4 points for every 1We count each token once, as in the final context. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Deep research over complex documents typically begins with OCR. DR PIXEL instead performs retrieval and reasoning directly over rendered pages. We study this setting with DRPIXELBENCH, containing 500 verifiable questions over 1.06M pages of scientific literature, and show that pagenative deep research consistently outperforms OCR-based pipelines across all tested models while using fewer tool calls, even without task-specific training. To close the remaining gap for openweight models, we introduce counterfactual credit reweighting, which weights teacher steps by their contribution to the gold answer and brings 27B model to GPT-5.4-level accuracy with lower search cost. These gains transfer to external benchmarks and non-scientific documents. More broadly, page-native deep research requires only document rendering rather than format-specific parsing, making it particularly attractive for private, layout-rich corpora such as financial or law documents where maintaining OCR and parsing pipelines is costly and brittle.

sections.title: B DR PIXEL INFERENCE DETAIL
sections.content: B.1 DEPLOYMENT AND ENGINEERING DETAIL Serving. GPT-5.4 is accessed through the OpenAI Responses API and Gemini-3.5-Flash through Vertex AI. Qwen3.6-27B, both the base model and our trained variants, is served with SGLang on four H200 GPUs in tensor-parallel mode at context length of 262,144 tokens. Reasoning is set to high for GPT-5.4 and Gemini-3.5-Flash, and enabled for Qwen3.6-27B. Following the Qwen model card, which warns that greedy decoding in thinking mode induces endless repetition, the open model is sampled at temperature 0.6, top-p = 0.95, top-k = 20 with presence penalty of 1.0; the proprietary models use provider defaults. All three run under an identical prompt, tool set and search budget. Halting at the tool call. The agent must stop generating the moment it emits tool call, so that the real retrieval result re-enters the context. For Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini-3.5-Flash we pass </call_tool> and </answer> as stop sequences. For GPT-5.4 the tools are declared as native functions and the API halts at the function_call item, with retrieved pages returned as image content in function_call_output. Carrying reasoning across turns. Qwen3.6-27B writes its <think> block in-band, so it is part of the conversation. For the proprietary models we echo the providers own representation verbatim, the thought_signature for Gemini-3.5-Flash and the encrypted reasoning item for GPT-5.4, carried in the request body with server-side retention disabled.

sections.title: C MORE ON DR PIXELTRAINED
sections.content: C.1 DR PIXELTRAINED TRAINING DETAIL Optimization. We fine-tune Qwen3.6-27B with LoRA of rank 32 and scaling α = 64, dropout 0.05, on every linear projection of the language model; the vision encoder stays frozen. Training runs for one epoch at constant learning rate of 1e4 with an effective batch size of 16, from four H200 GPUs at one sequence per device and four gradient-accumulation steps. We use bfloat16, FlashAttention, Liger kernels and padding-free packing, and set the maximum sequence length to 131,072 tokens. Applying the weights. Counterfactual credits are computed offline against the frozen base policy at two forward passes per step and written into the training file as per-message weight. Each assistant message is split at the boundary between its reasoning and its action so the two channels can carry different weights, and the trainer multiplies each messages token loss by its weight. The training step is therefore ordinary supervised fine-tuning at no extra cost, and the whole method sits in data preparation. Observation tokens are excluded from the loss in every arm. Training data. Training questions come from the same pipeline as the benchmark, taken before human annotation, over disjoint pool of papers, and no paper supporting training question supports an evaluation question. From 1,164 visual seed questions whose gold evidence anchored on table, figure, or equation, we sample six GPT-5.4 rollouts each under DR PIXEL, discard those with an incorrect final answer, and keep at most the three shortest trajectories per question, leaving 2,500 trajectories. The teachers trajectories are short, 5.1 searches per question, but heavy-tailed: under uniform token weighting the length seen by the gradient is E[n2]/E[n] = 9.3 rather than 5.1, and trajectories with at least ten searches are 15% of the data but 42% of the steps. Filtering for correctness also means every retained trajectory ends with the answer in its context, which evaluation does not guarantee.

Each variant changes one normalisation choice while the credits, the mask and the training recipe stay fixed. Columns are as in Table 4. Rescaling the weights costs reading accuracy, whether the mean weight is matched to the uniform baseline or the mass each trajectory contributes is equalised, while changing the pool step is ranked against does not help. Equation 4 fixes three properties that the counterfactual credit does not itself determine: the magnitude of the surviving weights, the pool of steps given step is ranked against, and how much mass single trajectory may contribute. Here we ablate on those three properties in Table 16 with the training recipe held fixed. Weight magnitude. Masking every step of non-positive credit zeroes about quarter of the steps and leaves the mean weight roughly third below the uniform baseline, so the weighted run effectively takes smaller optimisation steps, and constant factor on all weights is equivalent to change of learning rate. Restoring the mean to the baseline settles this: accuracy given the gold page falls from 68.7 to 63.1, the largest reading loss in the family, while the number of searches barely moves. Rank support. counterfactual credit is larger on hard questions, where deleting any step moves the likelihood of the gold answer substantially, so ranking against the whole training set imports question difficulty into step-level signal. The effect is measurable: the mean surviving weight of trajectory ranges from 0.65 at the tenth percentile to 1.70 at the ninetieth, so steps weight depends substantially on which trajectory it belongs to. We also try ranking step only against the other steps of its own trajectory, and only against the steps of the same questions rollouts. Both remove the leak, because step is then never compared with step from different question. Neither helps: within-trajectory ranking stays on par with the reference (50.1 vs. 50.9) and within-question ranking is 2.3 points lower, so the bias is real but harmless. Trajectory contribution. Equal mean weights do not equalise what trajectory contributes: its total weighted mass spans factor of about six between the tenth and ninetieth percentiles, since long or lightly masked trajectory supplies far more weighted tokens. Equalising that mass is the most aggressive variant we tried and the weakest result, five points below the reference. This is because light trajectory gets multiplied by large ratio. Numerical calibration is thus not where the credit acts. Rescaling the weights either does nothing or degrades reading, and changing the support of the rank does nothing at all. What remains is which steps the credit masks and how that mask is distributed along trajectory.

Share of the Data: trajectories and search steps by trajectory length; The dashed rules mark the average trajectory, which has 5.1 searches, and the same average weighted by how many steps each trajectory contributes, which is 9.3. Masked by Length: mask rate against trajectory length. Masked by Position and Surviving Weight: the same two quantities against position relative to the search that first retrieves page the final answer cites, marked by the dashed rule; that search is masked 2.5% of the time, the minimum of the panel. Figure 8: Share of questions that issue at least searches on DRPIXELBENCH. The harness stops trajectory at 20 calls, so the right-hand endpoint of each curve is that models exhaustion rate. DR PIXELTrained is the lowest curve from the twelfth search on and the only model that ends below 10%. Vanilla SFT and Gemini-3.5-Flash share shape: both stay above 75% for the first eight searches and then run out of budget rather than deciding to stop. Vanilla SFT and DR PIXELTrained see the same trajectories and differ only in how the loss is weighted, yet one issues 14.0 searches per question and the other 8.9 at the same page hit rate. We ask what the two models do differently at inference, and what in the loss produces it. At inference, the difference is stopping. Figure 8 plots the share of questions still searching after calls. The curves separate at once and never cross: by the fifth search DR PIXELTrained has finished third of its questions and vanilla SFT almost none. Per step, averaged over the first twelve searches, DR PIXELTrained stops with probability 10.2%, close to the untrained backbones 9.4% and GPT-5.4s 8.9%, while vanilla SFT stops with probability 4.4%. At that rate the expected trajectory is 22.8 searches, longer than the budget allows, so the cap is what ends third of its trajectories. The credit is not symmetric across the two channels. The credit is much harsher on reasoning than on search. As shown in Figure 7, it masks 62.6% of reasoning steps but only 24.5% of search steps. Only search reacts to trajectory length: almost nothing is masked on trajectories with single search, 0.2%, against 40.2% on trajectories that reach the budget, while reasoning stays between 51% and 68% whatever the length. The small slope reasoning does have is borrowed, since the cross-channel correction of 5.1 masks reasoning step whenever its query is masked. Length is

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: therefore handled by the search channel: longer trajectories lose larger share of their search steps, which is how the credit offsets the length bias, and reasoning follows along. The credit spares the search that finds the evidence and prunes the ones after it. In each trajectory we locate the first search that returns page the final answer cites, and measure the mask rate at each position relative to it. That search is almost never masked, 2.5% of the time, while every other search is masked between 15% and 42%. Among the steps that survive it also carries the largest weight, 1.25, against 0.7 to 0.8 for searches few steps later. Reasoning peaks one step further on, at 1.21. This position is never supplied to the method, so the pattern is emergent. Because almost every step the credit removes is issued after the evidence is already in context, the pruning suppresses continuation rather than retrieval, which is why the search count falls while the page hit rate does not.

sections.title: Agent system prompt
sections.content: Image input {retrieved page images, appended to every tool result} You are research assistant who answers questions about scientific papers through iterative reasoning and research. ## Process - Show your reasoning inside <think></think> tags. - Call tool with exactly: - When you have enough evidence, give the final answer with exactly: <call_tool name="TOOL_NAME">your query</call_tool> <answer>your answer</answer> - You may alternate between thinking and tool calls several times. (this is the most important rule) ## STOP after the tag Each turn you emit AT MOST ONE <call_tool> or ONE <answer>, and then you STOP WRITING. Do NOT write <tool_output> block yourself -- WE run the tool and send you the real results. Anything you write after the closing </call_tool> is discarded, and any tool output you invent is hallucination: the documents, page numbers and numbers in it are not real. Your turn looks like exactly this and nothing more: <think>What know so far, and what still need.</think> <call_tool name="TOOL_NAME">my query</call_tool> Your <think> stays visible to you for the rest of the session, so record in it any concrete value you read off an image -- that is your working memory. ## Tools (use ONLY these) {tools} ## Tool Output After each tool call the results come back to you in <tool_output> block: {obs} Results from EVERY tool call stay visible to you for the rest of the session -- you can re-read an image you retrieved earlier. ## Before you answer -- check yourself You may only answer when you can point to the SPECIFIC page/passage id you read the answer off (e.g. "P2_1"). Ask yourself: - Is the exact value/claim the question asks for actually VISIBLE in one of the results received? - If NO -> do NOT answer. Search again with different query. - "The retrieved page is about the right topic" is NOT enough. "I remember this paper" is NOT enough. Answering from memory when the evidence is not in front of you is the single worst failure mode here, because the answer will look confident and be about the wrong paper. ## CRITICAL ANSWERING RULES - Answer ONLY from evidence you actually retrieved this session. Do NOT answer from prior knowledge. - When the answer involves specific number, score, magnitude, threshold, or named model/method/dataset, you MUST retrieve it and state the SPECIFIC value(s). vague or directional answer ("generally better", "tends to improve", "competitive", "around X") when precise value exists is treated as WRONG. - NEVER guess or fabricate numbers, model names, method names, arxiv ids or document ids. If after searching you still cannot find the specific value the question asks for, say so explicitly -- do NOT invent one. - You start this session having retrieved NOTHING. The ONLY evidence that exists is what comes back inside real <tool_output> block that WE send you. If you have not yet received <tool_output>, you have no evidence and you MUST NOT answer -- search first. - Recalling the paper from memory is not evidence. If your answer would be the same without looking at the retrieved pages, you have not done the task. - For yes/no, comparison, trend, or regime questions: state the verdict/direction AND the supporting numbers behind it. Illustrative GOOD vs BAD answers (fabricated examples, NOT the real question): - "Does pruning hurt accuracy on the small model?" BAD : "Yes, pruning generally lowers accuracy somewhat." GOOD: "Yes -- accuracy drops from 79.3% to 74.1% at 50% sparsity  (Table 3)  , (vague -> WRONG) 5.2-point fall." - "Which retriever wins on the multilingual benchmark, and by how much?" BAD : "A single general retriever is competitive across languages." (names nothing -> WRONG) GOOD: "Retriever-Z leads, +1.8 nDCG@10 over the per-language baseline  (Table 4)  ." Rules: you may call tools at most {budget} times in total; after that you MUST answer. Issue focused queries. Read the returned passages/images carefully. sections.title: Answer grading prompt
sections.content: You STRICTLY grade an answer to question about research paper's figure/table/finding. The GOLD states SPECIFIC finding one can only know by reading the figure/table -- often exact numbers, named models/methods/datasets, or precise quantitative relationship. GRADING RULE: 1. If the GOLD contains specific numbers, named entities (models/methods/datasets), or precise magnitude, mark correct=true ONLY IF the PREDICTED answer states that SAME specific finding: the same numbers (within rounding) AND/OR the same named entities AND/OR the same precise relationship. Otherwise correct=FALSE. In particular: - Generic / directional answer that gets the trend right but OMITS the gold's specific numbers => WRONG. - Answer citing DIFFERENT numbers or DIFFERENT models/methods than the gold => WRONG (it guessed from prior knowledge, did not read the source). - Vague hedging ("levels off", "tends to", "generally", "competitive") in place of the gold's specific finding => WRONG. 2. If the GOLD has NO specific numbers/entities (a pure yes/no verdict or purely qualitative direction), then correctly matching verdict/direction is enough. Paraphrase of the SAME specific finding is fine; extra correct detail is fine; contradicted or reversed direction is always WRONG. answer_type = {atype} (verdict / comparison / trend / regime). CALIBRATION EXAMPLES: [CORRECT] GOLD: "No, it stays stable..." (no numbers) PRED: "No, ... remains bounded, avoids collapse" -> verdict matches, gold has no specifics. [CORRECT] GOLD: "operational factors; limiters = latent size and number of modules" PRED: "operational overhead; size and number of processed tensors" -> states the same specific finding. [WRONG] GOLD: "Jina-ColBERT-v2 within 0.4 nDCG@10 of mDPR-FT on MIRACL" PRED: "a single model such as CORA or mAggretriever is competitive" -> different models, none of the gold's specifics. [WRONG] GOLD: "EMOVA 72B trails on RealWorldQA 71.0 vs 75.4" PRED: "InternVL3-78B, Qwen-VL2.5-72B trail GPT-4o" -> different models, missing 71.0/75.4. [WRONG] GOLD: "edge vanishes: 66.6 vs 62.7 (Qwen2.5) but 70.3 vs 70.9 (Qwen3)" PRED: "the advantage diminishes" -> correct direction but NONE of the gold's specific numbers. [WRONG] GOLD: "rises 2->4, peaks 4, dips at 5" PRED: "levels off / plateaus" -> vague, misses the specific peak/dip. QUESTION: {q} GOLD ANSWER: {gold} PREDICTED ANSWER: {pred} First state the gold's KEY specific finding, then decide. Output ONLY: {"gold_key_finding": "<the specific finding the gold makes>", "correct": true or false, "reason": "<one sentence: does PRED state it?>"} Figure 11: The grading prompt. prediction is scored by majority of three independent votes from GPT-5.4-mini; an empty prediction is marked incorrect without being sent to the judge. Retrieval metrics do not pass through this prompt: page hit and document hit are decided by exact identifier match against the gold annotation.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Atomic fact extraction prompt (figure modality) Image input {cropped figure image} You are extracting fine-grained factual content from scientific paper FIGURE (the image). You are given the figure image, its caption, and the surrounding body text. Return STRICT JSON: { "overview": "<=2 sentences on what the figure shows", "atomic_facts": [ {"fact":"<one concrete, checkable fact READ FROM THE IMAGE>", "fact_type":"trendvaluecomparisonrankingstructureannotation", "stated_in_caption": truefalse, "stated_in_nearby_text": truefalse, "salience": 1-5} ] } Rules: - Facts must be things visible IN THE IMAGE PIXELS (values, trends, orderings, crossover points, error bars, sub-figure differences, color/legend mappings). - For each fact, judge honestly whether the SAME information is already explicitly stated in the caption / nearby text provided. - Prefer facts that are NOT stated in caption/text. 4-10 facts. CAPTION: {caption} NEARBY TEXT: {nearby} Figure 12: Atomic fact extraction, shown for the figure modality. Tables receive the same prompt with the OCRd cell text in place of the image; equations receive the LATEX source with no image; and body text is processed in chunks without caption or salience fields. The stated_in_caption and stated_in_nearby_text flags are what later let us keep only the facts reader could not obtain from the surrounding prose.

sections.title: Question generation prompt
sections.content: You read this (augmented) abstract. As working researcher, pick ONE thing you'd genuinely want to check whose precise answer needs figure/table/equation (a gap / head-to-head / where-it-breaks / dependency / feasibility / exception) -- NOT vague survey question, NOT trivial lookup. BE IMAGINATIVE -- go for NON-OBVIOUS, slightly surprising angle curious reader of the ABSTRACT would wonder about: an unexpected regime where the claim might break, counterintuitive comparison, "what's the catch", hidden tradeoff. Avoid the rote "does the proposed method beat the baseline?". The thing you ask about must be something the ABSTRACT itself raises (a claim/effect/tradeoff) -- NOT an internal experimental knob the abstract never mentions. Express it as an expectation ("I'd expect because Y"), pick the answer_type, give 2-3 grep keywords appearing in the paper's figure/table facts (dataset/method/metric words).{modhint} AUGMENTED ABSTRACT: {aug} Return JSON {"folk_belief":"...","intent":"...", "answer_type":"comparisontrendregimeverdict", "keywords":["..","..",".."]} Figure 13: Question generation. The model sees only the abstract, enriched beforehand with the atomic facts of Figure 12, and never the body of the paper, so the question is driven by what reader would wonder rather than by evidence already in view. Two further prompts, omitted here, turn the resulting expectation into precise question with short gold answer and then rewrite it in researchers voice.
